_note: Applied by videos/shared/narrate-walkthrough.mjs on top of showcase/SCRIPT.md, which is never edited. Only one kind of change here: trimmed narration. The script is written to be read, and at this voice's pace the twelve cues need about 4:40 of speech against a 2:52 recording — so each cue is cut to roughly 90% of the seconds its beat is on screen, keeping the point and dropping the elaboration. The cue START times are NOT overridden: record.spec.ts prints the moment each still is captured and SCRIPT.md is re-timed from that printout, so the script's own times are already the recording's. Re-derive these trims whenever the recording's pacing changes; `--no-synth` prints the per-cue window each one has to fit.

1.text: Someone on a live call needs what is true right now, not after it ends. This is Live, and the banner says plainly what it will not do.
1.note: 65w to 27w; Live is only on screen for 7s before the sample starts. The two promises the banner makes are on screen and legible, so the voice points at them rather than reading them out.

2.text: Press play. The brief is not redrawn from scratch on every line — the version number only moves forward when the server's own throttle decides a refresh is worth an LLM call. Watch it climb as the caller says more: a machine shop, binder jetting, a furnace, titanium and budget. Every claim is grounded, and the sources build up underneath.
2.note: 93w to 58w for a 22s window; the throttle explanation is the load-bearing part and is kept, its 'one refresh, not nine' illustration is not.

3.text: Next to the brief, the transcript and the session's own numbers: refreshes run, refreshes the throttle skipped, and how long the last one took.
3.note: 65w to 24w for a 12s window. The mock-versus-real latency comparison is dropped here; cue 5 already marks the content as sample.

4.text: Ending a session loses nothing — the brief, its sources and how it developed are kept. Conversations lists every call, and searching for something the caller actually said finds this one. Opening it shows the final brief, the full transcript, and every version the brief passed through, each timestamped and timed.
4.note: 72w to 51w for a 19s window; the scrolling directions are dropped, the viewer can see them.

5.text: Knowledge shows what a prospect is grounded in — sample content here, honestly marked. The Ask tester runs the same pipeline a live turn does and shows its work: nine steps, timed. Ask something it knows and the answer carries a citation; ask something it does not and it hands off.
5.note: 78w to 52w for a 19s window; the stepper is on screen, so the voice names it rather than walking it.

6.text: Before a prospect is trusted to answer it clears this gate: the same ten questions, through the same pipeline, right now.
6.note: 64w to 21w for an 8s window. 'All ten pass' is dropped — the gate chip on screen says it.

7.text: Quality checks all of that in aggregate. And when someone tries an injection, the guard trips first — the log keeps the reason, never the text.
7.note: 43w to 25w for an 8s window; the explanation of why that matters is dropped, the redacted row is visible.

8.text: Behind the product is an Operator panel for whoever runs the deployment, behind its own token. It sees the same session from the operator's side — every version the brief passed through, and how long each refresh took.

9.text: Settings is a reading screen until this browser proves it is an operator. The same token unlocks it in place, on this page.
9.note: 64w to 23w for a 7s window. The point that nobody is sent to a separate admin application survives in 'in place, on this page'.

10.text: Every setting this product reads from configuration is editable here. Type a partner's name into Branding: the preview repaints as you type, before anything is saved. Save, and the rail, the tab title and the action colour repaint underneath you — no reload, no restart. Reset the group and the environment's value comes straight back.
10.note: 89w to 57w for a 22s window. This is the pass's headline beat, so it keeps its whole argument: preview, save, repaint, reset.

11.text: Everything voice runs on ElevenLabs, configured from in here rather than their dashboard. No key on this deployment, so the page says so. Add one and this panel shows where it and the live agent disagree.
11.note: 100w to 34w for a 12s window. The tool, timeout, greeting and router prompt are all on screen and readable, so the voice makes the argument instead of listing them.

12.text: And everything you have watched the workspace do, an application can do. This explorer is built from the deployment's own OpenAPI document, so an operation cannot be added to the API and forgotten here. Find the voice turn, send it with the body already filled in, and the answer comes back with its citations and its timings — the same call the agent makes, written out as curl, ready to paste.
12.note: 91w to 70w for the closing 23s; the transport-agnostic line is dropped in favour of ending on something the viewer can see happening.
